Share: By Bronte McHenry Bronte McHenry November 4, 2021 ‍ One of our values is ‘we’re a startup too’. What this means is we tend to move fast, experiment, test, and ditch what isn’t working. It’s for this reason we’ve made changes to Open House
It’s for this reason we’ve made changes to Open House (formerly Office Hours) and the Accelerator application process.
What’s changed is there will no longer be a 1:1 mentoring component to Open House.
Instead, every startup that applies for the Accelerator will receive a 1:1 slot with one of our mentors.
Here is the what, why and how of our changes to Open House and the Accelerator application process .
What’s changed is there is no longer a 1:1 mentoring component.

When we began our Office Hours program, we wanted to make the idea of startup mentorship and investment much more accessible to a broader group of founders, especially those without warm networks in the industry.
Since then, the industry has come in leaps and bounds and many different organisations have followed on to open up their calendars for mentorship and investment intros throughout the year.
Looking ahead, we want to throw our energy and resources at two new challenges.
First, we want to offer more first round Accelerator interviews than ever before.
Q: Who are your mentors?
Our mentor community is made up of the most experienced founders and operators in the Australian and New Zealand startup ecosystem.
Every single one of our mentors is a handful of steps ahead of the founders who go through our Accelerator program, making them the best people to offer tailored mentorship.

Share: By Cara Davies May 3, 2022 In June 2021, we applied for Startmate's Winter21 Accelerator cohort. We did not get in. In December 2021, however, we applied again — and heard the exciting news that we were selected for the Summer22 cohort! In this article I will highlight the changes we made between applying in June and November, and explain the process of
Specifically, as first-time founders, Jake and I knew we had tonnes to learn, and were looking for mentors in product, investor relations and strategy.
What we did have: A great (albeit naive) we got this attitude; A recently closed pre-seed round; Recent market launch with a total of 200 users; and Dave as our third co-founder and CTO.
Written application and video -> 15-minute interview with a Startmate mentor -> Speed interview round -> 45-minute in-depth interview with three mentors.

To prep, I would recommend asking someone who has gone through the process before to do a test run with you ( HMU if you like ), chatting to one of your mentors about it, or getting a friend to test you.
Essentially, we would both act as mentors to the other person and do practice 10-minute interviews.
The mentors will have read your application but, just like you are doing 15 interviews, they are interviewing 15 companies, so the intro provides context.
If the mentors want more information they will ask for it.
Know that mentors will ask the same few questions (as there will likely be the same few big questions/concerns about your company).
Also the mentors are all really lovely — you don’t need to be super formal.
At the end of the day, accelerators are backing the team — so show what makes you an awesome founder.
45-minute in-depth interview with three Mentors In the final stage of the Startmate interview process you'll meet with 3 mentors for 45 minutes each.

Startmate is building the ecosystem that startups need to thrive in Australia and New Zealand. ‍ We bring the most ambitious founders , operators and investors together in our programs. Founders - we help you get started and invest in your company Operators - we help you launch and perform in your career in startups Investors - we help you work through
Startmate was founded in 2010, a time when Australia had latent creativity and potential, but lacked venture capital and accelerators to support it.
Everyone invested $10k into a micro-fund to invest in the next generation of early-stage founders, and started building a community of successful founders to support them.
Since ~2016, Startmate has become the Switzerland of VC in Australia and New Zealand.

Whilst we work closely with the Blackbird investment team, we have most VC funds in the countries investing, selecting and mentoring in our programs such as AirTree, SquarePeg, Main Sequence, Rampersand, Skip Capital, Grok Ventures, to name a few.
Where Australia and New Zealand will be known as the most innovative nations in the world.
We’re building an ecosystem within Startmate bottom-up instead of waiting for nationwide government or systemic changes.
We want to make Australia and New Zealand leaders in technology.
So the people who apply for our programs and memberships are generally people who are living, working, building & investing in Australia and New Zealand.
We have founders, mentors, investors, operators and partners scattered around the world.
Founders who apply and are accepted into our Accelerator program receive an investment of 120k.
Pre-product and pre-revenue.

Share: By Bronte McHenry Bronte McHenry February 28, 2022 ‍ Bec Rozencwajg is frank, warm and reflective — and has had a career that surprises, delights and impresses. It's filled with international travel, cultural immersion, government relations and a relentless
It's filled with international travel, cultural immersion, government relations and a relentless pursuit of meaning.
Some time at B Lab Australia and New Zealand, the Women Fellowship and an internship at Flying Fox Ventures later, she landed her dream job as Investment Manager of LaunchVic's Alice Anderson Fund.
Here's how she got there. ‍ Part one: Learning by doing "I'm Melbourne born and bred, but I've spent time living in Sydney, Japan and Canada," Bec tells me.
"My grandfather learnt the skill of a blacksmith in Germany, and it was what kept him alive through World War II and in concentration camps.
He managed to escape, and when he and my grandmother came to Australia post-war, he used that skill to set up a business of his own.
"When I came back to Australia, I decided to finish off my commerce/arts degree and complete a postgrad in Asian studies.
(And, oh the perks!) “I did a rotation with the government and international relations team, and I loved it.

I flew around the world encouraging airlines to fly into Melbourne and also saw the interplay of commerce and government from the other side.” Part three: Finding impact "Before I started a family, I decided to take some time off and learn about something I was quietly building a passion for: cheese," Bec tells me.
I took myself off to the US and France to spend time with some of the leading artisan producers.
That pursuit led me to a role with B Lab Australia and New Zealand (the not-for-profit behind the B Corp Certification) as their Head of Policy and Government Relations.

“Working in a co-working space with Impact Investment Group and Giant Leap Fund also exposed me to the world of finance and how investing with an impact lens could help support solutions that create a better future.

I also started investing in and advising impact focussed companies in their infancy.” Part four: The Women Fellowship and the Alice Anderson Fund "I came across the Women's Fellowship in the midst of working from home and home-schooling my kids during the pandemic," Bec says.

Here's why. Share: By Tom McLeod September 26, 2022 Beaming renewable energy anywhere on (or off) earth using lasers Decarbonising the planet is the greatest challenge of our lifetime. Renewable energy sources hold the key to reducing carbon in the atmosphere to a sustainable level where we can keep earth inhabitable and prosperous for many generations to come. However, while the planet has access to more energy from renewable sources than it could possibly

However, while the planet has access to more energy from renewable sources than it could possibly use, it has one huge problem: getting that energy to the right place, at the right time in the right quantities.

Typically this has been solved through building more transmission lines (getting energy from one place to another) or storage (mostly large batteries or hydroelectric dams) — but these approaches are very expensive, geographically constrained and slow to build.
But imagine if we could take energy generated at a solar farm in outback Australia and power factories in Europe.
Or use the energy from a wind farm in California to directly power electric planes in flight between San Francisco and Los Angeles.
Using a network of lasers, specialised mirrors and receivers, Aquila is able to deliver energy from where it is being generated, to where it is needed, anywhere on the planet.
Between the two of them they are the ‘swiss army knives of energy, space and lasers’ (side note, if you’re reading this Victorinox, that’d be a pretty sweet swiss army knife add-on).
Aquila’s technology can transcend the two largest barriers to the creation of an entirely renewable, global energy system.

The internet used commodity hardware and open protocols to allow as many machines as possible to join the network, and in turn, allowed the collective knowledge of humankind to be shared with anyone connected to that network.
We can think of Aquila like ‘the internet of energy’.
Billy and Nelson are combining existing technologies and components together in a novel way that will allow many players in the renewable energy space to be involved in this network of energy.
Just as the internet allowed data to be shared between any connected machines, so will Aquila allow the global sharing of clean energy between any connected devices. 🚀 Why now?
Mass electrification of the planet requires enormous amounts of renewable energy sources to be built in the coming years.

This creates an opportunity for Butter to provide much-needed peace of mind for consumers to build confidence that they won’t be left out of pocket if their valuable assets are damaged, stolen or destroyed.
